facts.claim: The Titanic struck an iceberg and sank on her maiden voyage
facts.context: She hit the iceberg late on 14 April 1912 and sank in the early hours of the 15th.
facts.goDeeper: The voyage was only four days old when she went down.

facts.claim: The wreck of the Titanic was located on the sea floor
facts.context: Found by a joint expedition led by Robert Ballard in September 1985, 73 years after the sinking.
facts.goDeeper: The search was partly cover for a secret US Navy mission to survey two sunken nuclear submarines.

facts.claim: People who died when the Titanic sank
facts.context: Roughly 1,500 of about 2,220 aboard died. Exact figures still vary between sources.
facts.goDeeper: Most died of cold rather than drowning; the water was around minus two degrees Celsius.

facts.claim: People aboard the Titanic when she sailed
facts.context: About 2,220 passengers and crew, well below her capacity of roughly 3,300.
facts.goDeeper: A national coal strike had cancelled other sailings, so she carried passengers transferred from other ships.

facts.claim: Lifeboats carried by the Titanic
facts.context: Twenty, with room for about 1,178 people — roughly half those aboard.
facts.goDeeper: That was more than British regulations required. The rules were based on ship tonnage, not passenger numbers, and were badly out of date.

facts.claim: Length of the Titanic
facts.context: About 269 metres, or 882 feet — among the largest moving objects yet built.
facts.goDeeper: A modern cruise ship like Icon of the Seas is longer and roughly five times her tonnage.

facts.claim: Time between striking the iceberg and going under
facts.context: About two hours forty minutes, from 11:40pm to 2:20am.
facts.goDeeper: Her designer Thomas Andrews inspected the damage and gave her about two hours. He was close.

facts.claim: Depth at which the Titanic wreck lies
facts.context: About 3,800 metres down, roughly 12,500 feet, off Newfoundland.
facts.goDeeper: That is deeper than most submarines can go; reaching it needs a purpose-built submersible.

facts.claim: Watertight compartments in the Titanic's hull
facts.context: Sixteen. She could stay afloat with four flooded. The iceberg opened five.
facts.goDeeper: The bulkheads did not extend high enough, so water spilled from one compartment into the next like an ice-cube tray.

facts.claim: Hours the Carpathia took to reach the survivors
facts.context: The Carpathia picked up the distress call and arrived at about 4am, some four hours later.
facts.goDeeper: Her captain shut off heating to the cabins to squeeze extra speed out of the engines.

facts.claim: The Titanic was launched at the Harland and Wolff yard in Belfast
facts.context: Launched 31 May 1911, then fitted out for nearly a year before her maiden voyage.
facts.goDeeper: She was launched without engines, funnels or interiors — just a hull, sliding into the water on tallow and soap.

facts.claim: Percentage of first-class women who survived
facts.context: Almost all first-class women survived. Among third-class women the figure was closer to half.
facts.goDeeper: Overall, about 75 percent of women aboard survived and about 20 percent of men.

facts.claim: Titanic's speed when she struck the iceberg
facts.context: About 22 knots, close to her maximum, in a region where ice had been reported.
facts.goDeeper: Ice warnings had come in by wireless all day. At least one was never passed to the bridge.

facts.claim: James Cameron's film Titanic was released
facts.context: Released in December 1997; it became the first film to take more than a billion dollars.
facts.goDeeper: Cameron made 33 dives to the real wreck. The footage in the film's opening is genuine.

facts.claim: The White Star Line officially advertised the Titanic as unsinkable
facts.context: The company never made that claim in its advertising. The phrase came from press coverage and trade journals, and grew in the retelling after the sinking.
facts.goDeeper: A 1911 shipping journal said she was 'practically unsinkable'. The qualifier did not survive.

facts.claim: The ship's musicians kept playing as the Titanic went down
facts.context: Multiple survivor accounts agree the band played on deck to the end. None of the eight musicians survived.
facts.goDeeper: What they played last is disputed; survivors named different tunes.

facts.claim: The Titanic broke in two before sinking
facts.context: Survivors said so at the time and were largely disbelieved. The 1985 discovery of the bow and stern lying far apart settled it.
facts.goDeeper: The two halves rest about 600 metres from each other on the sea floor.

facts.claim: Another ship was close enough to see the Titanic's distress rockets
facts.context: The Californian lay stopped in ice nearby. Her crew saw rockets but did not respond; her wireless operator had gone to bed.
facts.goDeeper: Both the British and American inquiries condemned her conduct, and the argument about how close she really was has never fully ended.

facts.claim: The Titanic had two nearly identical sister ships
facts.context: Olympic and Britannic. Olympic served for 24 years; Britannic sank in 1916 after striking a mine.
facts.goDeeper: One nurse, Violet Jessop, served aboard all three — and survived both sinkings.

facts.claim: The disaster led to new rules requiring lifeboats for everyone aboard
facts.context: The 1914 Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea required lifeboat places for all aboard and a continuous radio watch.
facts.goDeeper: SOLAS is still the treaty governing ship safety today, more than a century on.
